notes: \cpara{Recalls ``The Affect Heuristic,'' posted three days earlier, with two of its findings: benefits information lowering perceived risk of nuclear power, and analysts judging unfamiliar stocks as all good or all bad. Their sources are given there.}

\cpara{Defines the halo effect as the affect heuristic in social psychology. The evidence that follows is one long passage from Cialdini's \textsc{Influence}, a book for general readers; the post cites the studies only through it.}
\cpara{Cialdini on attractiveness: judges credit good-looking people with better traits without knowing it, and voters favor attractive candidates while denying it.}

\cfact{The review does not support two of the four traits. Eagly and colleagues found the differences between attractive and unattractive people ``largest for indexes of social competence; intermediate for potency, adjustment, and intellectual competence; and near zero for integrity and concern for others.'' Honesty and kindness fall in the last group. They also found the effect ``moderate'' on average and ``not as strong or general'' as ``what is beautiful is good'' suggests.}

\cfact{Cialdini's own notes give the source as an unpublished University of Toronto manuscript. I could not check it. Later published work finds the same direction on a smaller scale: in Finland, one standard deviation of rated beauty went with 20 per cent more votes for the average non-incumbent parliamentary candidate (Berggren, Jordahl and Poutvaara, 2010).}
\cpara{Cialdini on hiring and pay. The pay figure is broadly in line with Hamermesh and Biddle, who put the penalty for plain looks at 5 to 10 per cent and the premium for good looks slightly lower.}
\cpara{Cialdini on courts: a field study of sentences and a mock negligence trial.}

\cfact{The ratio is right (54 against 23 per cent avoided jail), but it is a raw comparison. The attractive defendants also faced less serious charges ($r = -.32$), which the jail figures do not control for. Allowing for seriousness, attractiveness still predicted shorter sentences, and Stewart called the relationship ``a weak one.''}
\cpara{Argues that attractiveness has no legitimate bearing on honesty, while honesty and intelligence may go together in fact. (On honesty and kindness, see the note on Cialdini's first sentence.)}
\cpara{Advises suspicion of anyone who seems good in every way, and of a world that sorts too cleanly into devils and angels.}

\cfact{What the post offers as a suspicion was the original finding. Thorndike named the halo effect in 1920 for ratings of the same person on ``intelligence, industry, technical skill, reliability,'' and of officers on intelligence, leadership and character, which correlated ``too high and too even.'' Like the post, Thorndike allowed that such traits really go together to some degree; his point was that the ratings were ``higher than reality, plus the attenuation due to erroneous judgments, could well give.''}
\cpara{The practical advice, drawn from the voting studies.}
